articles.title: Raptaioi, Evia – The Midnight Air-Spirit Wolf
articles.author: Titos Giochalas
articles.excerpt: A shepherd tale from Raptaioi where a spectral “Wolf” tears through the flock at midnight. Only heard and felt, never seen, the entity is treated with fear and immobility at the stroke of twelve.

image.alt: The spectral wolf of the Aerika at midnight, Raptaioi

content.value: The “Wolf” appears out of nowhere and savages the flock, by day or by night — though we ourselves never saw such a thing. Our grandfathers, now, had lived through a great deal. In our own time we have not set eyes on such phenomena. They used to say they had seen them with their own eyes.

They say that at midnight the shepherds keeping watch over the animals would suddenly bolt from where they were sitting. They felt fear. And then our grandfather would lift his head and say: “Ah! Something has just passed through the flock. It is the ‘Wolf’.”

If it is twelve at midnight, then above all you must not stir at all from where you are. Whatever you may hear, you must stay still, they said. They were careful. They did not go near. Because it was an “untimely” hour — it was not a natural one. It was the hour of the Aerika.

articles.title: The Air Spirits of Nigrita
articles.author: George Frederick Abbott
articles.excerpt: Nigrita locals blamed chronic illness on the Aerika (air spirits). An elder woman refused medical help for her lingering fever, convinced only the Aerika were responsible.

image.alt: Elderly woman in Nigrita speaking about the Aerika

content.value: In the same district I came across a number of people who put their bodily illnesses down to the malice of the “Spirits of the Air” (Aerika). One elderly woman complained to me of a low fever that had lasted a year. Naturally, I asked her whether she had consulted a doctor.
“What are the doctors going to do for you?” she answered me, put out. “It is an aeriko — and medicines do nothing against those.”

articles.title: The Whirlwind Charm and Alexander
articles.author: George Frederick Abbott
articles.excerpt: In Mesolakkia, Serres, a whirlwind called “anemosplada” is met with the chant “Alexander the Great lives and reigns.” The term links wind with the ancient word for dust.

image.alt: Whirlwind in rural Macedonia known as anemosplada

content.value:
In the district of Liakkovikia the whirlwind is called anemosplada, and while it passes the inhabitants are in the habit of whispering this strange refrain:
«He lives, he lives and reigns, Alexander the Great».

The word appears to be a compound, from ánemos (wind) and either spilás or splidós — or, more properly, spodós, that is ash, or better still, dust, as it appears in Herodotus (IV.172): tês chamáthen spodoû, “dust from the ground”.

articles.title: The Air Spirit at Giannitsa
articles.author: George Frederick Abbott
articles.excerpt: A caravan near Giannitsa was harassed by a mottled ghost-dog. Each time someone reached for it, the animal turned to air and later vanished by the Axios river.

image.alt: Caravan on the Macedonian plain where the ghost-dog appeared

content.value: Once, they say, a caravan was travelling by night towards Giannitsa, a town west of Thessaloniki. On the road a mottled little dog came up to them, appearing out of nowhere, and began tormenting the mules.

One of the drivers found the courage to climb down from his animal and try to catch it, but he failed utterly. This happened many times over, and each time, the moment he stretched out his hand, the little dog turned to air.
It did not stop harrying them until they reached the banks of the Axios (the Vardar), and there it vanished.

articles.title: The Goat-Spirit and the Bent-Neck
articles.author: George Frederick Abbott
articles.excerpt: In Galatista, Halkidiki, a villager earned the nickname “Stravosnichis” after trying to carry a stray goat that vanished into thin air, leaving him deformed.

image.alt: Galatista village in Halkidiki, site of the goat-spirit encounter

content.value: A villager in Galatista, in Chalkidiki, was known by the nickname Stravosnichis, and it is said that he owed his disfigurement to an incident of just this kind.
One evening, as he was coming back from the fields, he saw what he took for a harmless — if stray — goat grazing in a meadow.

He went up to it and hoisted it onto his shoulder, with the commendable intention of carrying it home as a gift for his wife. At that very moment, however, the goat vanished into the air, leaving him a memento that would mark him for the rest of his life.

articles.title: Fire Spirits near Isaakio
articles.excerpt: First-hand testimony of a smokeless fire seen in 1935 near Isaakio, Evros—suspected to be the work of Aerika.

image.alt: Field near Isaakio, Evros where a smokeless fire was seen

content.value: Since the talk has turned to the Aerika, Mr Theodoros Papachatzidis — about fifty years old, from Daniilio in Eastern Thrace, with schooling as far as the third grade — has something from his own experience to tell us.
Here near the little farmstead, a landowner and I were grazing the sheep. All this happened before the war, around 1935.
I was about fifteen at the time. As soon as night fell we looked and saw a fire in the green grass — but a fire with no smoke. We took fright and did not go near it.
The next morning we went back, and we found no trace of any fire.

sources.title: Thrakika vol. 45, Folklore of Isaakio Didymoteicho
